text: Samson went down to Timnah, and there he saw a woman, one of the Philistine daughters.
He came back up and told his father and mother, "I have seen a woman in Timnah, one of the Philistine daughters. Now get her for me as my wife."

But his father and mother said to him, "Is there no woman among the daughters of your own kin or among all my people, that you must go and take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?" Samson answered his father, "Get her for me, for she is the right one in my eyes."

versions.text: But his father and mother said to him, "Is there no woman among the daughters of your own relatives or among all our people, that you must go and take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?" Samson answered his father, "Get her for me, for she is the one who pleases me."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew reads "my people" (singular possessive), not "our people." Keeping the singular preserves the wording of the text; "kin" also renders אַחֶיךָ ("your brothers") a little more naturally than "relatives" for oral reading.

versions.text: But his father and mother said to him, "Is there no woman among the daughters of your own kin or among all my people, that you must go and take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?" Samson answered his father, "Get her for me, for she is the one who pleases me."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew idiom יָשְׁרָה בְעֵינָי ("she is right in my eyes") carries the sense of Samson's own judgment overriding his parents', which is thematically important in the Samson narrative. "The one who pleases me" conveys the general sense but loses the "in my eyes" imagery that recurs in Judges. The suggested wording keeps the idiom while reading smoothly aloud.

text: His father and mother did not know that this was from the LORD, who was seeking an occasion against the Philistines; for at that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.
So Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother. When they came to the vineyards of Timnah, a young lion came roaring toward him.
The Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him, and he tore the lion apart with his bare hands as one tears apart a young goat. But he did not tell his father or mother what he had done.
Then he went on down and spoke with the woman, and she pleased Samson.
Some time later, when he went back to marry her, he turned aside to look at the carcass of the lion, and there in it was a swarm of bees and honey.

He scooped the honey into his hands and ate as he went along. When he came to his father and mother, he gave them some, and they ate it too; but he did not tell them that he had taken the honey from the carcass of the lion.
His father went down to the woman, and Samson gave a feast there, as the young men customarily did.
When the people saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him.
Samson said to them, "Let me put a riddle to you. If you can solve it and tell me the answer within the seven days of the feast, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes.
But if you cannot tell me the answer, you must give me thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes." "Tell us your riddle," they said. "Let us hear it."
So he said to them: "Out of the eater came something to eat; out of the strong came something sweet." For three days they could not solve it.

On the seventh day they said to Samson's wife, "Coax your husband into explaining the riddle to us, or we will burn you and your father's household to death. Did you invite us here to rob us? Is that not so?"

versions.text: On the seventh day they said to Samson's wife, "Coax your husband into explaining the riddle to us, or we will burn you and your father's household to death. Did you invite us here to rob us?"
versions.explanation: The final הֲלֹא ("is it not so?") of the Hebrew is omitted. Adding it renders the full clause and sharpens the taunting tone.

text: So Samson's wife wept before him and said, "You only hate me; you do not love me. You have put a riddle to my people, but you have not told me the answer." "Look," he replied, "I have not told my own father or mother—why should I tell you?"
She wept before him all seven days of the feast, and on the seventh day he finally told her, because she kept pressing him. Then she told the riddle to her people.

versions.text: She cried on his shoulder all seven days of the feast, and on the seventh day he finally told her, because she kept pressing him. Then she explained the riddle to her people.
versions.explanation: "Cried on his shoulder" adds a detail not in the Hebrew (which is the same expression rendered "wept before him" in verse 16). Matching the wording of verse 16 keeps the narrative consistent for the ear. "Told the riddle" also mirrors the verb used throughout the chapter (הגד).

text: Before sunset on the seventh day the men of the town said to him: "What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?" And he said to them, "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have solved my riddle."

Then the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him. He went down to Ashkelon, struck down thirty of their men, stripped them of their garments, and gave the clothes to those who had explained the riddle. Burning with anger, he went up to his father's house.
And Samson's wife was given to the companion who had attended him.
